newsitem.title: FRANCE: U.S., France stress accord on non-Iraq issues.
newsitem.headline: U.S., France stress accord on non-Iraq issues.

text.p: The United States and France stressed their "convergence" on a broad range of foreign policy issues from NATO reform to Bosnia on Thursday, but sidestepped their sharp differences on Iraq.

After more than two hours of talks in Paris, U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher and French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette refused to take questions about a split between the two Gulf War allies over Washington's cruise missile strikes on Iraq this week, which France declined to support.
They said they wanted to meet French President Jacques Chirac later before addressing the issue.
"I want to emphasize the convergence of our ideas and policies," Christopher told a news conference, saying it was "the best meeting we've had, the most harmonious".

The two ministers said they were in step on plans to reform and enlarge the Atlantic Alliance, efforts to rekindle Middle East peace negotiations, the conduct of elections this month in Bosnia and efforts to rally international support for a global nuclear test ban treaty.
Christopher deflected repeated questions on Franco-American differences over Iraq.

Asked what would happen if allies declined to help the United States enforce a no-fly zone extended to just south of Baghdad, he said: "The United States intends to enforce the no-fly zone declared by the president."
Britain had said it would take part in the patrols but France has confined its aircraft to the old, smaller no-fly zone in southern Iraq.
Christopher said Washington would try to revive talks between the two feuding Kurdish factions and stressed the United States strongly opposed any Iranian support for Kurdish rebels against Baghdad.
De Charette rejected suggestions that Washington and Paris were at loggerheads on Middle East peace.
"There are not two different French and U.S. policies. There are convergent efforts by the two governments to get the peace process back on track," he said.

On Bosnia, he said Christopher had agreed on a French proposal for a two-year stabilisation period following September 14 elections. Details would be worked out by a ministerial steering committee in the autumn.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the ministers had a 15-minute private session on Iraq at the start of their meeting but then turned to other issues on which the two countries agreed.
